1a: **Sub-item 1a (2 points — meaning of a cumulative KPISet):** Deduct only when the answer leaves the concept of "cumulative" entirely unexplained — i.e., it never conveys, in any form, what a cumulative KPISet is or what role it plays. Do not require the specific merging mechanism: an answer earns the points if it gives any defensible account of the meaning, such as that the cumulative KPISet is built by merging two or more KPISets, or simply that it holds aggregate statistics covering the whole test run rather than a single interval. Likewise, do not deduct here when the answer does explain cumulative KPISets but explains them incorrectly — for example by describing them as deduplication, or as aggregation over a rolling/non-fixed time window. In that case the meaning was discussed, so 1a is satisfied; the inaccuracy is handled solely by sub-item 1b and must not be double-counted here. In short: no_deduct if any explanation of what "cumulative" means is present, correct or not; deduct only if the answer is silent on the concept.
1b:
Deduct the 3 points whenever the answer actually characterizes what a cumulative KPISet is and that characterization contains a materially incorrect claim of any kind. The two cases named in the rubric — describing cumulative KPISets as involving duplicates, or as aggregating over a non-fixed time period — are illustrative examples, not an exhaustive list; any other factual error in the description of a cumulative KPISet triggers the same deduction. In particular, treat statements that the cumulative KPISet aggregates data over the whole test run, from the start of the test to the present moment, or over a growing/expanding window as describing aggregation over a non-fixed time period, and deduct.

Do not deduct if the answer's description of cumulative KPISets is accurate, or if the answer never makes a substantive claim about what a cumulative KPISet is at all — e.g. it merely names cumulative KPISets, hedges ("it depends on your needs"), or frames the matter conditionally ("if it is specific to cumulative data..."). Silence or pure hedging is not an error and carries no deduction under this sub-item; there must be an asserted positive characterization that is wrong before the 3 points come off.
2a:
Award or deduct this 1 point on whether the answer actually gives the required explanation of `_compact_times()`: that it reduces memory use by combining/merging elements of the times data. To earn the point the answer must do two things at once. First, it must name the benefit in memory terms — memory, RAM, storage, or footprint. Framing the effect only as "improves performance," "speeds things up," "keeps the data manageable," or "reduces size," with no reference to memory, does not earn the point. Second, it must have substance beyond the function's name: a bare restatement such as "it compacts the times list" or a contentless gloss such as "it condenses the data" is not enough; the answer has to indicate that elements are combined/merged (so the stored series gets smaller) and that this is what saves memory. Tentative or hedged wording about this mechanism is acceptable — e.g. "this presumably merges points to limit memory" — and it may appear as an aside inside a discussion of the overhead or of the cumulative merge rather than as a standalone section; what matters is that the memory-optimization-by-combining idea is present.

Deduct the 1 point whenever that explanation is absent, and this includes answers that instead give a wrong account of the function — for example "it removes duplicate timestamps" or "it normalizes the times for statistical calculations." A wrong explanation is by definition not the required explanation, so this point is lost in addition to any separate deduction taken under 2b for incorrectness; do not treat the 2b deduction as covering this item. No_deduct only when the answer states, in memory/RAM/storage terms and with the combining-elements mechanism made explicit, what `_compact_times()` accomplishes.

CONFLICT: 2a_explanation_tied_to_cumulative_only_scope vs 2a_hedged_mention. The scope fork requires the memory/compaction rationale to be offered specifically as the reason to restrict the call to the cumulative KPISet (deduct if the answer recommends compacting every KPISet or leaves the scope open), while the hedged-mention fork says not to deduct whenever the memory-optimization-by-combining idea appears anywhere in the answer, including as an aside. An answer that explains memory savings via combining elements but recommends calling `_compact_times()` on every KPISet (or never specifies which sets to compact) is a no_deduct under the hedged-mention rule and a deduct under the scope rule.
2b:

Deduct the 2 points only when the answer makes an incorrect claim *about `_compact_times()` itself* and asserts it as fact — for example, stating that `_compact_times()` removes or handles duplicates, or that it is a necessary data-processing step for statistical calculations (as opposed to a memory optimization that combines elements). Scope the check strictly to the answer's description of `_compact_times()`: a duplicates claim made about cumulative KPISets or about the merge step belongs to the cumulative-KPISet sub-item and must not be double-counted here, so if the `_compact_times()` description itself is clean, do not deduct. Likewise, treat only assertions as disqualifying — explicitly hedged, speculative, or "one possibility is…" statements about duplicates or statistical necessity, and statements that raise such a reading only to reject it, do not trigger the deduction. When a disqualifying asserted claim does appear anywhere in the answer's treatment of `_compact_times()`, deduct the full 2 points even if the answer also correctly identifies `_compact_times()` as a memory optimization that combines elements; that correct content earns credit under the other sub-items but does not offset or shield this deduction.
